cues: Welcome to Claude Artifacts — the complete visual guide.
Prepared by Sara Salem.
In this video, you'll discover every type of artifact Claude can create, and learn how to build your own — step by step, from the first idea to a published, shareable app.
Let's start with the difference between a normal chat answer, and an artifact.
A normal chat answer is text inside the conversation. It's great for explanations, but it's hard to reuse, edit, or share as a finished piece of work.
An artifact is different. It opens in its own window, next to the chat. It can be a working app, a web page, a document, or a diagram — and you can edit it, download it, and share it.
Think of the chat as your conversation with Claude, and the artifact as the thing you're building together.
So, what exactly is an artifact?
An artifact is a substantial, standalone piece of content that Claude creates in a dedicated panel beside your chat.
It's rendered live — so code runs, pages display, and buttons actually work.
Every change you ask for creates a new version, so you can always go back.
And when it's ready, you can copy it, download it, or publish it with a link.
Here's how an artifact comes to life.
First, you describe what you want in a prompt.
Claude generates the content or the code.
The artifact panel renders it live, right next to the chat.
You iterate, asking for changes until it's exactly right.
And finally, you share it with others.
Claude can create several types of artifacts. Let's look at each one.
Code artifacts hold scripts and programs in any language — like Python, JavaScript, or SQL — with syntax highlighting, ready to copy.
Documents are written in Markdown — perfect for reports, guides, plans, and study notes.
Web pages are single-file HTML, with CSS and JavaScript — like landing pages, forms, and small tools.
SVG graphics are scalable vector images — logos, icons, illustrations, and infographics that stay sharp at any size.
Diagrams are created with Mermaid — flowcharts, sequence diagrams, timelines, and more.
And React components are fully interactive apps, with state, charts, and modern styling — like dashboards, games, and calculators.
Let's look closer at one type: a Mermaid diagram. It's simple text that turns into a visual flowchart.
The first line declares the diagram type — here, a flowchart that flows from left to right.
Each box is a step in the process, like a new customer order.
Curly brackets create a decision, like: is the item in stock?
And arrows connect everything, with labels for each path. Claude writes this for you — you simply describe the process in plain words.
Now, let's build an artifact step by step. Step one: plan before you prompt.
First, make sure artifacts are turned on in your Claude settings. They're available on the web, desktop, and mobile apps.
Next, pick the right type for your goal — a document, a web page, a diagram, or an interactive app.
Then define the purpose and the audience. Who will use it, and what should it help them do?
And sketch the layout in your head, or on paper: what sections, buttons, or charts should it have?
Step two: write a clear prompt. Here's an example for an interactive budget tracker.
Start by naming the artifact type and the goal — here, a React artifact for tracking a budget.
List the features you need — adding entries, showing a balance and a chart, and saving data between visits.
Describe the design — the style, the colors, and that it should work well on mobile.
And mention the data — for example, start with a few sample expenses, so you can see it working right away.
Step three: Claude generates the artifact. Let's peek at the code it writes.
At the top, it imports what it needs — like React's state hook, and a charting library.
Then it stores the data in state, and calculates values like the balance automatically.
Next, it builds the interface — the title, the balance, and the chart.
And it styles everything with modern CSS classes. You don't need to write any of this yourself — but you can read and edit it in the code view.
Step four: preview and test your artifact.
Switch to the preview tab, to see the live, working app — here, the budget tracker's spending by category, using its sample data.
Click every button, enter different values, and try it on a small screen.
Then switch to the code tab whenever you want to understand or copy the code.
Testing early helps you spot what to improve in the next step.
Step five: iterate with follow-up messages. This is where artifacts really shine.
You ask for a change — for example: add a monthly budget limit, and show a warning when I go over it.
Claude updates the artifact, keeping everything else that already works.
A new version is saved automatically.
And you can compare versions, or go back to an earlier one at any time. Keep iterating until it's exactly right.
Step six: master editing and versions.
Level one is targeted edits. Select a specific part of the artifact, and ask Claude to change just that piece.
Level two is bigger changes. Ask for a new feature or a redesign, and Claude rewrites what's needed.
Level three is version history. Every change is saved, so you can browse earlier versions, and restore the best one.
This lets you experiment freely, without ever losing good work.
Step seven: fix errors in seconds. Sometimes, generated code has a bug.
When an error appears in the artifact panel, you'll see a clear message.
Click the try fixing button.
Claude reads the error message, and finds the cause.
It updates the code with a fix.
And the artifact works again — usually in just one step. If not, describe what you see, and Claude will keep improving it.
Step eight: take your artifact further, with advanced features.
AI-powered artifacts can call Claude from inside the app — turning a simple page into a smart tool, like a tutor or a writing assistant.
Persistent storage lets your artifact remember data between sessions, so users don't lose their work.
Connectors can link artifacts to your everyday tools, through MCP.
And when you share an AI-powered artifact, people use it with their own Claude account — so there are no API keys to manage.
Step nine: publish and share your artifact.
Click publish, to create a link to your artifact.
Share that link with your team, your clients, or the world — depending on your plan and settings.
Anyone with the link can open it, and interact with it right away — no setup needed.
And they can remix it, creating their own copy to customize in their own Claude conversation.
With artifacts, you can build almost anything. Here are some ideas.
Interactive dashboards, games, and landing pages.
Data visualizations, flashcards and quizzes, and handy calculators.
Flowcharts, and personal planners. If you can describe it, you can build it.
Here are six best practices for great artifacts.
One: name the artifact type in your prompt, so Claude knows exactly what to build.
Two: be specific about features, design, and data.
Three: start simple, then add features one at a time.
Four: test every button and input in the preview.
Five: use version history to experiment safely.
And six: review the content before you share it publicly.
Let's recap in one line: describe, build, share.
Claude artifacts turn your ideas into real documents, diagrams, and apps — right inside the conversation.
